title: Choking or blocked airway

differential.label: Food or a floating object blocking the airway. Emergency
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. In flight a floating object or food crumb can be breathed in.

differential.label: Partial blockage with forceful coughing
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Let the person keep coughing and watch closely.

differential.label: Throat spasm after something touched the vocal cords
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Needs flight surgeon review.

differential.label: Severe allergic reaction with throat swelling
differential.note: Working idea only. This is not a diagnosis. Use the allergy card if there was no object.

tests.title: Can they speak or cough?
tests.instruction: Ask: are you choking? Note yes if they can speak or cough hard.

tests.title: Oxygen level after the airway is clear
tests.instruction: Clip the pulse oximeter on a finger. Enter the oxygen level.

tests.title: Pulse after the airway is clear
tests.instruction: Read the pulse from the oximeter or count it for 1 minute. Enter the pulse.

tests.title: Breathing rate after the airway is clear
tests.instruction: Count breaths for 1 minute. Write down the number.

immediateSteps.title: Ask if they are choking
immediateSteps.instruction: Ask: are you choking? Ask: can you speak? Look for hands at the throat.

immediateSteps.title: If they can cough or speak, let them cough
immediateSteps.instruction: Do not hit or squeeze them. Stay next to them. Act at once if the cough gets weak or they cannot speak.

immediateSteps.title: If they cannot speak or breathe, call the crew
immediateSteps.instruction: Shout for help. Start the next step now.

immediateSteps.title: Brace yourself behind them
immediateSteps.instruction: Get behind the person. Hook your feet into a foot restraint or handrail. Wrap your arms around their waist.

immediateSteps.title: Give thrusts
immediateSteps.instruction: Make a fist. Put the thumb side just above the navel, well below the breastbone. Grab the fist with your other hand. Pull in and up fast. Repeat until the object comes out or they pass out.

immediateSteps.title: If they pass out, start CPR
immediateSteps.instruction: Call every crew member. Restrain the person if you can. Start chest compressions. Look in the mouth before each breath. Remove an object only if you can see it and it is loose.

immediateSteps.title: After the object comes out
immediateSteps.instruction: Keep the person still. Check oxygen level and pulse. Send the case to the flight surgeon, even if they feel fine.

cautions: This card is not a diagnosis. It gives no doses. Do not reach blindly into the throat. Thrusts can injure, so every person who got thrusts needs a flight surgeon review. Bracing with foot restraints is a team suggestion; no source tests the Heimlich maneuver in weightlessness. Airway tools (AMBU bag, airways, forceps, cutting the neck) are for trained crew under flight surgeon direction only.
sourceNote: Researcher card, Pulseframe Batch 2, 2026-11-15. Built from NASA IMM data, the 2001 ISS medical checklist (historical), the NASA Human Research Roadmap choking page, the DGLRM/ESAM microgravity CPR guideline and MedlinePlus first aid. Not a current NASA procedure. Pending second-person safety review.
redFlagsCallGround: Any choking episode, even if the object came out.
In the next days: a cough that does not go away, fever, trouble swallowing or speaking, shortness of breath or wheezing.

timeLimits.item: If the person cannot speak or breathe, act at once. Do not wait for the ground.
Watch for cough, fever, trouble swallowing, shortness of breath or wheezing for the next days. These can mean the object went into the lung.
NOT FOUND: how many minutes without air before brain injury, from a source we could quote. Looked in MedlinePlus 000049, HRR choking page, Hinkelbein 2020.

whenGroundUnavailable.status: NOT FOUND (the choking page has no loss-of-signal note)
whenGroundUnavailable.detail: The 2001 ISS choking procedure is written as an emergency the crew does at once, with no step that waits for the ground. Other 2001 ISS pages say to begin treatment during loss of signal and call the surgeon as soon as possible. No current public rule was found. Looked in: 2001 ISS checklist, HRR choking page, OCHMO briefs, Hinkelbein 2020.
firstAidThatNeedsNoGround: Thrusts until the object comes out or the person passes out.
CPR if the person passes out.
Record oxygen level, pulse and breathing rate with the time once the airway is clear.
Send the case as soon as the link returns.

proposedKeys.reason: Already proposed in new-measurement-keys.csv. Not in keys.ts yet, so the breathing rate test has no inputKey.

candidateItemNotes: No inventory.json item treats choking. The 2015 kit list and the 2001 checklist name an AMBU bag, nasal and oral airways and Magill forceps, but none of these are in inventory.json. equipmentIds lists equipment.json ids used by the tests and steps.
gaps: No source tests back blows or abdominal thrusts in weightlessness. Bracing advice is team inference.
No source covers self-rescue when a crew member chokes alone.
The 2001 ISS procedure uses a blind finger sweep; current MedlinePlus advice says do not grasp a lodged object. The card follows MedlinePlus. Needs flight surgeon review.
AMBU bag and airway tools are not in inventory.json.
